title: Nutrition & Exercise
tagline: How food and movement build the body — the honest, evidence-based version.
description: What calories, protein, carbs and fat actually do; how muscle grows and shrinks; why the scale lies; cardio versus weights; exercise as metabolic medicine; protein and muscle as you age; and a clear-eyed pass through the myths. Plain language, current evidence, for everyone. Educational only — not medical advice.

concepts.title: Energy balance — the honest version
concepts.summary: Weight tracks calories in versus calories out. That law is real — but the two sides push on each other, so 'just eat less' rarely works alone.

cards.h: The one law that always holds
cards.md:
Store more energy than you burn and you gain weight; burn more than you store and you lose it. This is thermodynamics — it is not up for debate, and no food is magically exempt.

Your body spends energy three ways:

- **Resting metabolism** — keeping you alive at rest. This is the big one: roughly **60–70%** of daily burn.
- **Movement** — exercise *and* fidgeting, standing, walking around (called NEAT). Surprisingly variable person to person.
- **Digesting food** — you burn calories processing meals (the *thermic effect*). **Protein costs the most to digest.**

Here is what the simple calories-in-calories-out picture hides: **the two sides are connected.** Cut calories hard and your body defends itself:

- Resting metabolism **drops** — you burn less at rest.
- Hunger hormones (ghrelin) **rise**; fullness hormones (leptin, GLP-1) **fall**. You get hungrier.
- You unconsciously move less.

This is *metabolic adaptation*, and it is why willpower alone so often loses. It also explains why the GLP-1 medicines work — they act on that hunger side of the equation directly. Energy balance is the law; the hormones decide how hard it fights you.

questions.prompt: Roughly what share of your daily calorie burn is just resting metabolism — staying alive at rest?
feedback: Far too low — resting metabolism is the single biggest slice.
Higher than that — exercise is usually the smaller piece.
Correct — roughly two-thirds of daily burn keeps you alive at rest; exercise is a smaller slice on top.
Not quite — movement and digestion still take a real share.

questions.prompt: When someone cuts calories sharply for a while, what does the body typically do in response?
options: Speeds up resting metabolism to burn the fat faster
Lowers resting burn and raises hunger — it defends the weight
Nothing — the body has no way to respond
feedback: The opposite — the body slows down to conserve energy.
Correct — metabolism drops and hunger rises. This *metabolic adaptation* is why dieting on willpower alone is so hard.
It responds strongly — that adaptation is the whole difficulty.
'Damage' overstates it; the slowdown is largely reversible, not permanent.

questions.prompt: Which part of a meal costs the MOST energy just to digest and process?
feedback: Fat is the cheapest to store, not the costliest to process.
Carbs sit in the middle.
Correct — protein has the highest thermic effect; a real slice of it is burned off in digestion, one reason protein helps with weight.
They differ — protein is clearly the most expensive to process.

concepts.title: The three macronutrients — what each one is for
concepts.summary: Protein, carbohydrate and fat are the three fuels. Each does a different job: protein builds, carbs power, fat runs the slow systems.

cards.md:
Protein breaks down into **amino acids**, the bricks your body uses to build and repair — muscle, enzymes, antibodies, hormones. Unlike fat, you **cannot store spare protein** for later, which is why a steady daily supply matters.

Protein's superpowers:

- **Most filling** of the three — it quiets appetite best.
- **Costs the most to digest** — you keep less of what you eat.
- **Preserves muscle** when you are losing weight.

Good sources: meat, fish, eggs, dairy, beans, lentils, tofu, soy. About **0.8 g per kg of body weight** is the bare minimum; **1.2–1.6 g/kg** suits anyone active or losing weight.

cards.h: Carbs and fat — power and the slow systems
cards.md:
**Carbohydrate** is your fastest fuel. It breaks down to glucose and powers hard effort and the brain. Extra is stored as *glycogen* in muscle and liver. The useful split is by quality:

- **Whole** carbs (vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains) come wrapped in fibre — slow, filling, steady.
- **Refined** carbs (sugar, white flour) hit fast and leave you hungry again.

**Fat** is the most energy-dense fuel (9 calories per gram vs 4 for protein and carbs) and it is *essential* — some vitamins (A, D, E, K) only dissolve in fat, and your hormones are built from it. Favour unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, fish); go easy on the heavily processed kind. **No macronutrient is the enemy** — the dose and the quality are what matter.

questions.prompt: What is the key thing that makes dietary protein different from fat in how your body handles it?
options: You cannot store spare protein for later the way you store fat
Protein cannot be used for energy
Protein is only found in meat
feedback: Protein has 4 calories per gram — it is not calorie-free.
Correct — there is no protein 'storage tank,' so a steady daily intake matters; fat, by contrast, stores easily.
It can be burned for energy, though that is not its main job.
Beans, lentils, dairy, eggs and soy are all rich sources too.

questions.prompt: Fat contains how many calories per gram compared with protein and carbohydrate?
feedback: Fat is the most energy-dense, not the least.
Protein and carbs are 4; fat is higher.
Correct — fat packs 9 calories per gram, more than double protein or carbs, which is why fatty foods add up fast.
Fat is the most calorie-dense fuel there is.

questions.prompt: Comparing a bowl of lentils to a sugary drink with the same calories, what is the main difference?
options: The lentils have fibre — slower, more filling, steadier blood sugar
They are nutritionally identical since the calories match
The sugary drink is more filling
The lentils have no usable energy
feedback: Correct — 'a calorie is a calorie' for weight math, but *whole* carbs come with fibre that slows digestion and fills you up; refined sugar does neither.
Same calories, very different effect on hunger and blood sugar.
Refined sugar is famously *un*-filling — it leaves you hungry again.
Lentils are a genuine fuel and a protein source besides.

concepts.title: How muscle grows and shrinks
concepts.summary: Muscle is a live balance between building and breaking. Training plus protein tips it toward growth; doing nothing tips it toward loss.

cards.md:
Muscle is never static. Every day two opposite processes run:

- **Muscle protein synthesis (MPS)** — building new muscle protein.
- **Muscle protein breakdown (MPB)** — tearing old protein down.

Whether you gain or lose muscle is simply which one wins over time. Two levers push the balance toward **building**:

1. **Resistance exercise** — lifting, pushing, pulling against load. The mechanical tension is the *signal* to grow.
2. **Protein / the amino acid leucine** — the *raw material*, and itself a switch that flips synthesis on.

Signal **plus** material together beat either one alone. This is the same sarcomere — the sliding-filament engine — you meet in the animation; training builds *more* of these units.

cards.h: Use it or lose it — and it is fast
cards.md:
Take the signal away and the balance flips toward breakdown **quickly**. In strict bed rest, healthy people can lose muscle within **days**. Immobilise a limb in a cast and it visibly shrinks in a couple of weeks. Muscle is metabolically expensive, so the body sheds what it is not asked to use.

The good news is the same law in reverse: the stimulus does not need to be heroic. Meaningful effort — carrying, climbing, lifting something genuinely challenging a few times a week — is enough to hold the signal 'on.' The muscle you keep is the muscle you keep *asking for*. This 'use it or lose it' rule becomes the whole ballgame as we age — the next concept but one.

questions.prompt: Whether you gain or lose muscle over time comes down to the balance between which two processes?
options: Building muscle protein (synthesis) versus tearing it down (breakdown)
feedback: Both matter, but they are not the muscle balance itself.
Correct — muscle is a live tug-of-war between synthesis (MPS) and breakdown (MPB); whichever wins over time decides the outcome.
Neither of those is the core muscle-balance equation.
That is body composition, a different axis from the muscle balance.

questions.prompt: To tip the balance toward BUILDING muscle, you need both a signal and raw material. What supplies each?
options: Cardio for the signal, water for the material
Resistance exercise for the signal, protein/leucine for the material
Sleep for the signal, fat for the material
Neither is needed — muscle grows on its own
feedback: Cardio is great for the heart but is not the main muscle-growth signal.
Correct — mechanical tension from resistance work is the *signal*, and protein (rich in leucine) is the *material* and itself a growth switch. Together they beat either alone.
Sleep helps recovery, but the growth signal is mechanical load.
Without a load signal and material, the balance drifts toward loss.

questions.prompt: How quickly can a healthy person start losing muscle during strict bed rest or a limb in a cast?
options: Within days to a couple of weeks
feedback: Far faster than that — disuse acts quickly.
Correct — remove the signal and the balance tips to breakdown within days; muscle is expensive, so the body sheds what it is not asked to use. 'Use it or lose it' is literal.
Muscle very much shrinks without use — that is the whole point.
It happens at any age when the stimulus is removed.

concepts.title: Body composition — why the scale lies
concepts.summary: Your weight is fat plus muscle plus water plus bone. Two people at the same weight can look and function completely differently.

cards.md:
Step on a scale and you get **one number for everything at once** — fat, muscle, bone, water, even the food in your gut. It cannot tell them apart, and that makes it a poor judge of health or progress.

Watch the animation: with resistance training and enough protein, **fat mass falls while muscle rises a little**. Add them up and total weight barely moves — the scale looks 'stuck' while the person is visibly leaner, stronger, and healthier. This is *body recomposition*, and it is invisible to a scale.

It also explains the reverse trap: crash-dieting can drop the scale fast, but if much of that loss is **muscle and water**, you are lighter and worse off.

**Body Mass Index (BMI)** — weight scaled for height — is a screening tool for populations, not a verdict on an individual. It cannot see composition, so a muscular athlete can register as 'overweight' while a sedentary person of 'normal' BMI carries risky fat around the organs.

More telling day to day:

- **Waist size** — fat around the middle (*visceral fat*, wrapped around the organs) is the metabolically dangerous kind.
- **How your clothes fit** over weeks.
- **Strength and stamina** — are the stairs getting easier?

The lesson: judge the **direction of change and how you function**, not a single morning's number. Muscle is the organ you *want* to keep, even when it hides your weight loss.

questions.prompt: Why is the bathroom scale a poor judge of health on its own?
options: It reports one number for fat, muscle, bone and water combined — it cannot tell them apart
Weight has nothing to do with health
feedback: A good scale is accurate — the problem is *what* it measures.
Correct — the scale lumps everything together, so it misses body recomposition (fat down, muscle up) entirely.
It works for everyone; it just cannot see composition.
Weight matters — but *what* the weight is made of matters more.

questions.prompt: During successful 'body recomposition,' what happens to the scale?
options: It barely moves, even though fat fell and muscle rose
feedback: Not necessarily — that is the point; the scale can miss real change.
Correct — fat down plus muscle up nets to little scale change, so a stuck number can hide a body that transformed. Judge direction and function, not one morning's weight.
It stays roughly flat, not sharply up.
It is real and well documented, especially in beginners.

questions.prompt: Which is the metabolically DANGEROUS kind of fat, and a better everyday gauge than BMI?
options: Fat under the skin of the arms; measured by height
Visceral fat around the organs; gauged by waist size
All fat is equally harmful; BMI is the only measure
feedback: Limb fat under the skin is comparatively benign.
Correct — visceral fat wrapped around the organs drives metabolic risk, and waist size tracks it far better than BMI, which cannot see composition at all.
Fat location matters a great deal, and BMI is blind to it.
Excess visceral fat is genuinely harmful.

concepts.title: Cardio vs weights — you need both
concepts.summary: Aerobic exercise trains the heart and the endurance machinery; resistance exercise builds muscle, strength and bone. They are not interchangeable.

cards.md:
**Aerobic ('cardio')** — walking, cycling, swimming, running. Sustained effort that makes you breathe harder. It trains:

- the **heart** to pump more per beat,
- the **mitochondria** (your cells' power plants) to multiply,
- **endurance** and cardiovascular health.

**Resistance ('strength')** — lifting, pushing, pulling, bodyweight work. Brief, hard efforts against load. It builds:

- **muscle size and strength**,
- **bone density** — the pull of muscle on bone tells it to stay strong (critical against osteoporosis),
- resting metabolism, because muscle is active tissue.

cards.h: Why one cannot replace the other
cards.md:
Run marathons and you can still be weak and lose bone. Only lift and your heart-lung endurance lags. They train **different systems**, so the strongest evidence — and the biggest drop in risk of dying early — comes from doing **both**.

A widely used weekly target:

- **150 minutes** of moderate aerobic activity (a brisk walk counts), *or* 75 minutes of vigorous, **plus**
- **2 sessions** of resistance training hitting the major muscle groups.

You do not need a gym or heroics — brisk walking plus a handful of hard efforts against something heavy will do it. The best exercise is genuinely the one you will keep doing. Consistency beats intensity you cannot sustain.

questions.prompt: Aerobic exercise and resistance exercise mainly train different systems. Which pairing is right?
options: Cardio builds bone density; weights build the heart
Cardio trains the heart and mitochondria; weights build muscle, strength and bone
Both do exactly the same thing
Neither affects the heart or muscle
feedback: Reversed — weights build bone, cardio trains the heart.
Correct — they drive different adaptations, which is exactly why they are not interchangeable and the best results come from doing both.
They overlap a little but train largely different systems.
Each strongly affects its own system.

questions.prompt: Why does the pull of muscle on bone during strength training matter?
options: It has no effect on bone
It signals bone to stay dense and strong — key against osteoporosis
It only matters for young athletes
feedback: It matters a lot — bone responds to mechanical load.
Correct — loading tells bone to maintain density, so resistance training is a frontline defence against the bone loss of ageing.
Loading strengthens bone, it does not weaken it.
It matters most for older adults, who are losing bone.

questions.prompt: What does the standard weekly activity target recommend?
options: About 150 min of moderate cardio PLUS 2 resistance sessions
feedback: Cardio alone leaves strength and bone untrained.
Correct — roughly 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity plus two strength sessions a week captures both systems; a brisk walk counts.
Weights alone leave endurance and heart health behind.
The evidence points strongly the other way — movement lowers risk.

concepts.title: Exercise as metabolic medicine
concepts.summary: A contracting muscle pulls sugar out of the blood without needing insulin — a second door that insulin resistance cannot rust shut.

cards.h: The second door into the cell
cards.md:
In the Diabetes module you met **GLUT4** — the glucose doors that insulin orders to the muscle-cell surface. Here is the beautiful part: **muscle can open those same doors by itself, without any insulin.**

When a muscle contracts, an energy-sensing enzyme called **AMPK** switches on and sends GLUT4 to the surface directly. Glucose pours in and blood sugar falls — through a completely separate route from the insulin key.

That is why a single brisk walk after a meal measurably lowers blood sugar, and why exercise works **even when insulin resistance has set in**: it reaches a door that resistance cannot block. The animation is the same GLUT4 mechanism from Diabetes, opened by a different hand.

The benefits compound well beyond that single glucose dip:

- **Insulin sensitivity rises for a day or more** after a session — the insulin key itself works better afterward.
- **Mitochondria multiply** (*mitochondrial biogenesis*) — more power plants means the muscle burns fuel more cleanly.
- Regular training **shrinks visceral fat** and lowers blood pressure and inflammation.

This is why exercise is described, without exaggeration, as one of the most powerful **metabolic medicines** we have — and it is free. For someone with, or heading toward, type 2 diabetes, muscle is not just for looks: it is a large, trainable **glucose sink** that keeps working even as the insulin signal fades. *(Educational only — anyone on glucose-lowering medication should coordinate exercise changes with their clinician, since activity and medication both lower blood sugar.)*

questions.prompt: How can a contracting muscle lower blood sugar even when insulin is not working well?
options: It cannot — muscle needs insulin for everything
Contraction activates AMPK, which opens GLUT4 doors directly, no insulin required
It makes the pancreas release more insulin
feedback: Muscle has a genuine insulin-independent route — that is the key point.
Correct — the exercise-sensing enzyme AMPK sends GLUT4 to the surface on its own, a second door that bypasses insulin entirely.
The effect is inside the muscle itself, not via extra insulin.
Sugar goes into the muscle as fuel, not into bone.

questions.prompt: Beyond the immediate glucose dip, a training session tends to do what for insulin?
options: Raises insulin sensitivity for a day or more — the insulin key works better afterward
Has no lasting effect at all
feedback: Exercise improves the insulin system, it does not destroy it.
Correct — insulin sensitivity climbs for 24 hours or more after exercise, so the key itself works better; the benefit outlasts the workout.
The after-effect is exactly what makes exercise 'metabolic medicine.'
The opposite — cells respond to insulin *better* after training.

questions.prompt: Why is muscle described as a trainable 'glucose sink,' especially valuable in type 2 diabetes?
options: It is a large tissue that keeps pulling glucose from the blood even as the insulin signal fades
feedback: Muscle is in fact the body's biggest glucose store (as glycogen).
Correct — muscle is a big, exercise-responsive sink for blood glucose that keeps working through the insulin-independent door, which is why keeping muscle matters so much in type 2 diabetes.
Muscle lowers blood sugar by taking glucose up.
Muscle is the major site of glucose disposal, not fat.

concepts.title: Protein and muscle as you age
concepts.summary: After midlife muscle quietly slips away — a condition called sarcopenia. Enough protein plus resistance training is the proven defence.

cards.md:
From around the **30s–40s**, adults lose muscle at roughly **0.5–1% a year**, accelerating later — a condition called **sarcopenia** (Greek for 'poverty of flesh'). It is one of the biggest, most preventable drivers of frailty in later life.

Why it matters far beyond appearance:

- **Falls and fractures** — weak legs and poor balance are how independence is lost.
- **Metabolic health** — less muscle means a smaller glucose sink, nudging toward diabetes.
- **Resilience** — muscle is the body's protein reserve for surviving illness, surgery, and hospital stays.

Older muscle also suffers *anabolic resistance*: it responds less to a given amount of protein, so older adults need **more**, not less.

Two moves, well supported by evidence:

1. **More protein than the textbook minimum.** The old RDA of 0.8 g/kg is a floor to avoid deficiency, not a target for healthy ageing. Research supports **1.0–1.2 g/kg or more** for older adults, and spreading it **across meals** (each with enough of the amino acid *leucine* to flip the muscle-building switch), rather than loading it all at dinner.

2. **Resistance training.** This is the non-negotiable one — the mechanical signal that tells the body to keep the muscle. It works at **any** age; studies of people in their 80s and 90s show real strength gains in weeks. Protein without the signal is bricks with no builder.

The encouraging truth: sarcopenia is one of the most reversible parts of ageing. Muscle you train for is muscle you keep — the 'use it or lose it' rule, now with the stakes of independence.

questions.prompt: What is sarcopenia?
options: The age-related loss of muscle mass and strength
feedback: It is about muscle, not a vitamin.
Correct — sarcopenia is the slow loss of muscle with age (~0.5–1%/yr from midlife), a leading and largely preventable driver of frailty.
It affects skeletal muscle, not the heart specifically.
It is the opposite — loss, not excess.

questions.prompt: Because older muscle shows 'anabolic resistance,' how should protein intake change with age?
options: Drop below the RDA — older adults need less
Rise above the old 0.8 g/kg minimum, spread across meals
feedback: The opposite — needs go up, because the muscle responds less per gram.
Correct — anabolic resistance means older muscle needs *more* protein (≈1.0–1.2 g/kg+), spread across meals with enough leucine each time, to trigger the same building.
The 0.8 floor is a deficiency threshold, not an ageing target.
Protein matters *more* with age, not less.

questions.prompt: Which single intervention is the non-negotiable defence against age-related muscle loss?
options: Resistance training — the mechanical signal to keep the muscle
Nothing works after a certain age
feedback: Protein is the material, but without a load signal the balance still drifts to loss.
Correct — resistance training is the essential signal, and it works even in one's 80s and 90s. Protein is the bricks; training is the builder telling the body to keep them.
Under-eating accelerates muscle loss — the wrong direction.
Strength training produces real gains at every age tested.

concepts.title: Cutting through the noise
concepts.summary: The nutrition and fitness world runs on hype. Here are the stubborn myths and what the evidence actually says — the honest version.

cards.md:
- **'Muscle turns into fat if you stop training.'** Impossible — they are different tissues. Muscle *shrinks* and fat may *grow*; one does not transmute into the other.
- **'You can spot-reduce belly fat with crunches.'** No. You cannot choose where fat comes off; it leaves the whole body in its own order. Crunches build the muscle *under* the fat.
- **'Protein wrecks your kidneys.'** Not in healthy people — no good evidence of harm. (Those with existing kidney disease are a real exception and should follow medical advice.)
- **'Detox teas / cleanses flush out toxins.'** Your liver and kidneys already do this, continuously and for free. 'Detox' products mostly lighten your wallet.
- **'Carbs (or fat) are inherently fattening.'** Neither. *Excess calories* are fattening, from any source.

cards.h: The short list that actually works
cards.md:
Strip away the noise and the durable, evidence-backed basics are almost boringly simple:

- **Enough protein**, spread across the day.
- **Mostly whole foods** — plants, and minimally processed things — with room for what you enjoy.
- **Resistance training + regular movement.**
- **Sleep and stress** — poor sleep raises hunger hormones and eats into muscle recovery. It belongs on the list.

On supplements: the vast majority are unnecessary. The rare ones with solid evidence are **creatine** (safe, well-studied, helps strength and possibly brain) and **protein powder** — which is just a convenient food, not magic. Vitamin D can help if you are deficient. Everything promising fast, effortless results is selling the promise, not the result. **Consistency in the basics beats every shortcut.**

questions.prompt: Can targeted ab exercises like crunches 'spot-reduce' belly fat?
options: Yes — crunches burn the fat directly above the muscle
No — you cannot choose where fat comes off; crunches build the muscle under it
Only if you do 100 a day
feedback: Fat loss is not local to the working muscle — this is a durable myth.
Correct — fat leaves the whole body in its own genetically set order; you cannot target a spot. Crunches strengthen the muscle *beneath* the fat, they do not melt the fat above it.
Volume does not change the biology — spot reduction still does not happen.
Age does not unlock spot reduction; nobody can do it.

questions.prompt: What does the evidence say about high protein intake and kidneys in HEALTHY people?
options: No good evidence of harm in healthy people (existing kidney disease is a real exception)
Protein is filtered by the liver, not the kidneys, so it is irrelevant
feedback: That claim is not supported for people with healthy kidneys.
Correct — the 'protein harms kidneys' fear does not hold up in healthy people; the genuine exception is those with pre-existing kidney disease, who should follow medical guidance.
The kidneys do handle protein's by-products — but healthy ones cope fine.
Plant and animal protein are both fine for healthy kidneys.

questions.prompt: Which two supplements actually have solid evidence behind them?
options: Creatine and protein powder (a convenient food, not magic)
feedback: Detox and fat-burner products are exactly the hype to ignore.
Correct — creatine is safe and well-studied for strength, and protein powder is simply convenient food; most other supplements are unnecessary. Vitamin D helps only if you are deficient.
A few (creatine, protein, vitamin D when deficient) do have real evidence.
Trends are the opposite of evidence — the basics are what endure.
